Remote Patient Monitoring (RPM)

Care That Continues Between Visits, Not Just During Them

Remote patient monitoring uses connected devices, blood pressure cuffs, glucose meters, pulse oximeters, weight scales, to collect a patient's health data outside the clinic and send it to their care team. A chronic condition doesn't wait for the next scheduled appointment to change, and RPM gives providers visibility into that change as it happens, not weeks later.

RPM is also billable under specific CPT codes, but only when the program is run correctly: devices set up and transmitting data, a minimum number of monitoring days met each month, and time spent reviewing data properly documented. Programs that skip any of these steps either fail to bill compliantly or leave revenue on the table entirely.

PMEX manages the full RPM workflow: patient enrollment, device setup and data integration, ongoing monitoring support, clinical documentation, and CPT-compliant billing, so the program runs cleanly from a clinical and financial standpoint alike.

RPM Billing Codes

Four Codes, Each With Its Own Requirement

CPT 99453

Setup & Education

Initial device setup and patient education on use, billed once per episode.

CPT 99454

Device Supply

Monthly device supply with data transmission, requiring a minimum number of monitoring days.

CPT 99457

First 20 Minutes

First 20 minutes of clinical staff time spent on monitoring and management each month.

CPT 99458

Additional 20 Minutes

Each additional 20-minute block of monitoring time beyond the first, billed as needed.

RPM Program Setup

Devices, workflows and staff roles configured before the first patient enrolls.

Monthly Reporting

Enrollment, monitoring days and billing status reported every month.

Remote Patient Monitoring: Frequently Asked Questions

Patients with chronic conditions that benefit from close tracking, hypertension, diabetes, COPD or heart failure, are common candidates, though any condition where trend data between visits changes clinical decisions can qualify.

Connected blood pressure cuffs, glucose meters, pulse oximeters and weight scales are the most common, all transmitting data automatically so patients don't have to manually log readings.

Current CMS rules require at least 16 days of transmitted data within a 30-day period to bill the device supply code. PMEX tracks this threshold automatically for every enrolled patient.

Clinical staff at your practice review the data and make care decisions. PMEX supports the workflow, documentation and billing around that review, not the clinical judgment itself.

Yes. Device data flows into the EHR and practice management system you already use, so readings appear directly in the patient's chart without manual entry.
